title: AI Can Expand Coordination Capacity, but It Cannot Automatically Decide What Deserves Protection
summary: Algorithms and AI can scale high-frequency, complex coordination, but computational capacity alone cannot determine value priorities, cost allocation, or final legitimacy.
shortAnswer: Algorithms and AI can scale high-frequency, complex coordination, but computational capacity alone cannot determine value priorities, cost allocation, or final legitimacy.
displayQuestion: AI Can Expand Coordination Capacity, but It Cannot Automatically Decide What Deserves Protection

blocks.text: Artificial capability first changes the scale of coordination. Resource matching, signal filtering, risk tracking, and large volumes of repeated decisions can run at frequencies far beyond a single human position. Explicit rules can be automated, and more complex information can be assembled with the help of artificial systems.

But the ability to participate in coordination is not the same as final coordination authority. Computation can show which option is faster, cheaper, or better aligned with a defined objective, but it cannot by computation alone decide which values should take priority, whose costs are acceptable, or whether an efficient outcome is still unacceptable.

Algorithms are not neutral mirrors of reality. Choosing what to measure, how to classify, and which objective receives more weight already contains design decisions. If measurable variables continuously gain more decision power, difficult-to-quantify relationships, meanings, and long-term consequences can gradually lose their place. Automation amplifies the information structure it inherits, including its blind spots.

Mature artificial coordination therefore needs boundaries and exit paths. When inputs move outside known conditions, risk becomes too high, signals conflict, or current rules cannot represent the situation adequately, the system should be able to stop automatic handling and return the judgment to a more appropriate position. “Not enough authority to decide automatically” must be a legitimate state.

As artificial systems become more autonomous, important questions include who may change the objective, who can stop the whole process, who can force degradation, and whether affected people retain meaningful ways to understand, appeal, and reopen the structure. Humans do not need to inspect every high-speed machine coordination step, but when consequences enter human reality, responsibility and legitimacy cannot disappear merely because execution has been automated.

blocks.heading: Key judgment
blocks.statement: Artificial capability can expand the range of coordination; it cannot turn “computed” into “ought” by itself.

blocks.question: Which coordination decisions are suitable for automation, and which must preserve an entry point for reinterpreting values, boundaries, and responsibility?
